extracted.intended_audience: MIT inventors (faculty, researchers, staff, and students) submitting invention disclosures and seeking university technology transfer/licensing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for MIT inventors on assessment, filing, protection, marketing, and commercialization of university-owned inventions through the Technology Licensing Office (TLO). Covers patentability, commercialization assessment, disclosure risks, timelines, costs, marketing, licensing, product development, and revenue distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (USPTO)
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States Patent Office (USPTO) grants patents to inventions that meet three main criteria. The invention has to: Be novel; Be non-obvious; Have utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO will determine whether or not the technology fits the criteria for patentability after you submit your disclosure. The patentability review is performed in consultation with patent attorneys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial assessment — unmet needs and competing solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of unmet needs or problems the technology might solve and any competing solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO evaluates whether the invention addresses an important unmet need and how it compares to existing alternatives when assessing commercial licensing potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial assessment — potential market applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of potential market applications for the technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment includes identifying realistic end-use markets and whether the invention can be applied in those markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial assessment — potential costs and market support
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of potential costs associated with the solution and whether it may be supported by the market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO weighs development and production costs against market willingness to pay; high costs may impede licensing interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial assessment — commercialization challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of challenges that may impede sustainable commercialization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO looks for scientific, engineering, regulatory, supply-chain, or market-adoption barriers that could prevent successful productization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial assessment — industry openness to licensing early-stage tech
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a relevant industry is open to licensing of early-stage technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO assesses industry norms and whether potential licensees are willing to take on early-stage inventions versus only mature technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial assessment — stage of development / reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The technology’s stage of development or reduction to practice is considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More developed technologies (prototypes, validated data) are generally more attractive; TLO evaluates readiness for licensing and additional development needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: TLO decision authority
rubrics_metrics.description: While TLO works closely with inventors, the TLO will make the ultimate decision about whether or not a patent application is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventor input is solicited, but licensing officers and TLO leadership determine which cases proceed to filing based on combined patentability and commercial potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect against public disclosure before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Posters, abstracts, or presentations describing an invention to the public are considered public disclosures, which can prevent patenting in most countries if the public disclosure occurs prior to filing a patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The US allows inventors to file a patent application for up to one year after public disclosure, but it is best to disclose technology to the TLO well in advance of any public disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use confidentiality agreements and MTAs for outside disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: For extra protection, any presentation of the invention to a party outside of MIT should be covered by a nondisclosure agreement (NDA), a tangible property agreement, and/or an Incoming Material Transfer Agreement (MTA) if applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO recommends NDAs/MTAs to reduce risk of losing patent rights when discussing inventions with outside parties prior to filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect multi-year patent prosecution timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The process of obtaining a patent with the USPTO occurs over several years—the average US utility patent application is pending for about three years, though inventors in the biotech and computer fields should plan on a longer patent prosecution period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan project timelines and commercialization expectations around multi-year prosecution and allowance processes; issued patents are typically enforceable for 20 years from the initial filing that resulted in the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect substantial patenting costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a non-provisional US patent application may cost between $10,000 and $20,000 and the cost of obtaining an issued patent may cost a total of $40,000 to $50,000, in addition to maintenance fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursuing patents in other countries is expensive; TLO carefully reviews commercial potential before dedicating resources to prosecution and foreign filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration with outside patent counsel during application and prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: Once TLO has determined a patent application should be filed, the TLO will collaborate with an outside patent counsel to support the process, assuring access to patent specialists in diverse technology areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent counsel may continue to seek inventor input on technical issues during patent prosecution; inventors should be prepared to work with counsel and licensing officers throughout prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why to pursue patents — exclusivity to justify investment
rubrics_metrics.description: To justify dedication of resources to development and commercialization, a company often seeks exclusive commercial rights to an invention in its end use market application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO carefully reviews commercial potential because the need for commencing a patent filing often precedes finding a licensee; they look for efficient ways to seek early protection for promising inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing — identify and target appropriate licensees
rubrics_metrics.description: TLO will identify and market MIT-protected inventions to appropriate companies that have the expertise, resources, and business networks to bring the technology to market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO uses many sources and strategies (including existing relationships) to find potential licensees; an inventor’s personal connections to industry counterparts and entrepreneurs may support matching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing materials and non-confidential disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensing officers may generate marketing materials detailing non-confidential information packages to share with potential company licensees or potential investors, including an in-depth listing on the website and one-page summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting materials may include a one-page summary outlining benefits, publications, published patent applications or issued patents to help demonstrate value to potential licensees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor involvement in marketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Once interested licensees are identified, an inventor may be the best person to describe the details of the invention and its technical advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most successful technology transfer results are obtained when the inventor and the licensing professional work together as a team to market and promote the technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee selection — preference for companies committed to commercialization
rubrics_metrics.description: TLO pursues commercial license agreements with companies that are committed to commercializing MIT’s inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference is given to licensees who will actively develop, invest in, and bring the technology to market rather than passive holders of rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect licensee product development activities
rubrics_metrics.description: After obtaining a license, the licensee will continue development which may include additional testing, prototyping for manufacturability, durability and integrity, and further development to improve performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation for training, installation, and marketing is often created; benchmarking tests are often required to demonstrate product/service advantages and position the product in the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: TLO ongoing monitoring of licensee progress
rubrics_metrics.description: The TLO maintains an ongoing working relationship with each licensee over the term of the license agreement to monitor progress toward development and commercialization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TLO tracks milestones and commercialization progress to ensure licensed technologies are advancing toward market impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of licensing revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: Revenue from licensed technology can include annual licensing fees, royalties derived from sales, and equity received under a license agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Royalties may occur years after licensing; equity is typically liquidated at a liquidation event (e.g., public offering or acquisition). License revenues paid to inventors are generally taxable and reported as Form 1099 income.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue distribution policy and deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductions from Gross Revenue include a 15 percent administrative fee to cover TLO operating costs, any unreimbursed patent costs or other IP protection/defense costs, and payments due to third parties such as joint owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Net Revenue is then distributed 33 percent to inventors/authors/contributors (divided equally unless they agree in writing otherwise). The remaining Net Revenue is distributed evenly across the MIT General Fund and to academic departments, centers and labs after adjustments to recover unreimbursed patent costs. Yearly royalty revenue distribution occurs once a year, usually in the first quarter of the following MIT Fiscal Year.
